Skip the manifest and the sensor is invisible to operators even if it runs. go Adding the sensor to DefaultRegistry ```go // runner/internal/harness/registry.go func DefaultRegistry() *SensorRegistry { r := NewSensorRegistry() r.RegisterFactory(SensorFactory{ Manifest: GoTestManifest(), Constructor: NewGoTestSensor, }) // …existing sensors… r.RegisterFactory(SensorFactory{ Manifest: FilesChangedManifest(), Constructor: NewFilesChangedSensor, }) return r } ``` ## Test and ship Sensor tests follow the pattern in ` sensor_gotest_test.go ` — construct the sensor, feed it a ` SensorInput ` with controlled fixture data, assert the resulting ` SensorResult `. Keep the test hermetic: don't shell out to real tools, don't hit the network. Sensors run on every pipeline tick; a flaky sensor is worse than no sensor. Rebuild the runner: ` cd runner && go build ./cmd/backplane-runner `. Publish the new binary (or image) to wherever your runners pull from; operators re-register on their next restart and the new sensor shows up in the pipeline builder's sensor picker, populated from the heartbeat manifest. Add its name to a stage's ` sensors: [] ` array to start gating on it. > [!IMPORTANT] > The manifest is the contract > > > > > > The backend validates pipeline configs against the sensor manifest shipped in the last heartbeat. A stage referencing a sensor name the runner hasn't registered will fail validation when the config saves. If you add a sensor, rebuild, and deploy, make sure every runner rolls before you publish a pipeline that depends on the new sensor — a mid-rollout operator can save a config the stale runners can't honor. > [!HONEST] > You can't add a sensor at runtime > > > > > > Operators configuring a pipeline can *reference* sensors. They can't *define* them. Adding a sensor requires a Go file, a build, and a runner redeploy. For a platform that markets itself on extensibility this is uncomfortable, and we know it. The compile-time boundary exists because sensors run with full filesystem and network access inside the runner process — a runtime-authored sensor is a sandboxing problem we haven't solved yet. > [!FUTURE] > The declarative sensor DSL > > > > > > The long-horizon goal is a YAML-authored sensor spec an operator can write in the pipeline builder: a command to run, an exit-code mapping, a regex or JSON path to extract findings, and a pass/fail rule. The interpreter would execute the sensor in a sandboxed subprocess with a fixed filesystem view and no network. This unblocks operator-defined ` tsc --noEmit `, ` ruff `, ` eslint `, and any other toolchain without asking us to ship a new runner binary. Scoped, not scheduled — no ETA.

Use to inspect wiring before adding or removing edges. ### What the model sees ``` List a card's dependency edges both ways: depends_on (prerequisites) and blocks (dependents). ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | UUID of the board. | | ` card_id ` | required | Full UUID of the card, or a unique id prefix (≥4 chars). | ### Gotchas - depends_on = this card's prerequisites; blocks = cards waiting on this one. - card_id accepts a short id prefix (≥4 chars), resolved against this board. - Edges carry the other card's title, status, and column type — often enough without fetching each card. ### Example prompt ``` Show me everything the '' card on the board depends on and every card it blocks. ``` ### Related tools [get_card_dependency_status](#tool-get_card_dependency_status) [add_card_dependency](#tool-add_card_dependency) [remove_card_dependency](#tool-remove_card_dependency) [validate_board_dependencies](#tool-validate_board_dependencies) ## validate_board_dependencies readRead-onlyIdempotentIn default hand ` mcp__valaris__validate_board_dependencies ` Check a whole board's dependency graph for cycles, conflicts, and dangling edges. Use before sprint planning or when cards seem stuck for no clear reason. ### What the model sees ``` Check a board's whole dependency graph for faults. Archived templates keep serving bound boards; there is no hard delete. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` ref ` | required | The workspace template's row UUID (or slug). | | ` archived ` | optional | True to archive (default), false to restore to the listing. | ### Gotchas - Archiving removes it from the catalog listing but keeps it serving boards already bound to it. - There is no hard delete on purpose — a board bound to a deleted template would render nothing on its next iteration. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, archive the loop template <ref> in <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [list_loop_templates](#tool-list_loop_templates) [get_loop_template](#tool-get_loop_template) <a id="tool-list_loop_template_versions"></a> ## list_loop_template_versions readRead-onlyIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__list_loop_template_versions ` The template's published history, newest first: version number, publish timestamp, and changelog note. ### What the model sees ``` List a template's published versions, newest first: version, timestamp, note. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` ref ` | required | A system template slug, or a workspace template's row UUID. | ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, show the version history of the loop template <ref> in <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [restore_loop_template_version](#tool-restore_loop_template_version) [publish_loop_template](#tool-publish_loop_template) <a id="tool-restore_loop_template_version"></a> ## restore_loop_template_version write ` mcp__valaris__restore_loop_template_version ` Stage a published snapshot as the current draft. It does NOT republish — review, then publish separately. ### What the model sees ``` Stage a published version as the current draft. Does not republish. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` ref ` | required | The workspace template's row UUID (or slug). | | ` version ` | required | The published version number to stage as the draft. | ### Gotchas - Restoring is a draft edit, not a rollback: the published version stays put until you publish the restored draft. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, restore version 2 of the loop template <ref> in <workspace> as a draft. ``` ### Related tools [list_loop_template_versions](#tool-list_loop_template_versions) [publish_loop_template](#tool-publish_loop_template) <a id="tool-get_board_loop_binding_raw"></a> ## get_board_loop_binding_raw readRead-onlyIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__get_board_loop_binding_raw ` Raw view of a board's template binding: template, version, rendered slot values, and drift — the authoring state behind get_board_loop, the effective loop config. ### What the model sees ``` Raw view of a board's template binding: template, version, rendered slot values, drift — the authoring state behind get_board_loop, which is the effective loop config. 404 `not_bound` when the board's prompts are raw. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | UUID of the board; the board's slug also works. | | ` include_diff ` | optional | True to also fetch the unified prompt diff and slot delta between the bound version and the current one. | ### Gotchas - get_board_loop carries only the slim template ref — enough to render "bound to X", not enough to re-render. This is the read that answers "what would I edit?". - Returns 404 not_bound when the board's prompts are raw rather than template-rendered. - include_diff costs a second round-trip and is skipped entirely when the binding reports diff_available: false — a board with no drift has nothing to diff. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, call get_board_loop_binding_raw for the <board> board in <workspace> to see which template and slot values its loop renders from. ``` ### Related tools [get_board_loop](#tool-get_board_loop) [set_board_loop](#tool-set_board_loop) [get_loop_template](#tool-get_loop_template) <a id="tool-apply_loop_template_fixes"></a> ## apply_loop_template_fixes writeDestructiveIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__apply_loop_template_fixes ` Apply the named setup fixes from a fit report (create a missing column, add a label) and return the freshly recomputed report. ### What the model sees ``` Apply named fixes from a fit report, then return the fresh report. Idempotent per fix (`skipped_already_satisfied`); unknown fix ids are 422 before anything applies; a frozen board 409s. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | UUID of the board; the board's slug also works. | | ` template_ref ` | required | A system template slug, or a workspace template's row UUID. | | ` fix_ids ` | required | The fix_id values from get_loop_template(view='fit'), e.g. "create_column:done". Only these are applied — nothing implicit. | ### Gotchas - Admin + human keys only — the backend 403s runner callers, because a loop runner reshaping the board that governs it is a privilege escalation. - Idempotent per fix: an already-satisfied requirement returns skipped_already_satisfied, never an error. - Unknown fix ids are rejected wholesale (422) before anything is applied; a frozen board 409s. - Acts on the DRAFT half, like the report it consumes: a board can be prepared for a contract that has not been published yet. A column is inert until something binds to it. > [!DANGER] > Danger zone > > > > This mutates board structure — it can create columns and labels. Run get_loop_template(view='fit') first and pass only the fix_ids you intend. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, apply the create_column:done fix from the <template> fit report to the <board> board in <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [get_loop_template](#tool-get_loop_template) [set_board_loop](#tool-set_board_loop) <a id="tool-export_loop_template"></a> ## export_loop_template compositeRead-onlyIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__export_loop_template ` Export one loop template as a portable envelope — profile, prompts, slots, rails. Feed it to import_loop_template to promote a proven loop elsewhere. ### What the model sees ``` Export a template as a portable `loop_template` envelope for import_loop_template. System templates export too. `data.leak_findings` carries lint hints as warnings; export always succeeds. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the SOURCE workspace. | | ` template_ref ` | required | A system template slug, or a workspace template's row UUID. | ### Gotchas - Exports the DRAFT half, so work in progress is shareable — publish first if you mean to share the runnable version. - Exporting a SYSTEM template is allowed and marked data.is_system_origin: it is the supported way to fork a shipped loop. - data.leak_findings carries the same repo-fact hints get_loop_template(view='lint') reports, as warnings only — the export always succeeds. _hint counts them. - Member-gated, not admin-gated: anyone who can read the template in the manager can export it. ### Example prompt ``` Export the <template> loop template from <workspace> with export_loop_template and tell me whether any repo-specific facts would travel with it. ``` ### Related tools [import_loop_template](#tool-import_loop_template) [get_loop_template](#tool-get_loop_template) <a id="tool-import_loop_template"></a> ## import_loop_template compositeDestructive ` mcp__valaris__import_loop_template ` Import a loop_template envelope as a DRAFT in this workspace. Previews by default; dry_run=false commits. Admin/human keys only — runners get 403. ### What the model sees ``` Import a `loop_template` envelope as an unpublished DRAFT. Dry-run by default: returns {action, findings, diff_summary, leak_findings}, writes nothing; dry_run=false adds `template_id`. A matching slug overwrites that draft (`action` updated|created). Over ~64 KB, POST /loop-templates/import directly. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the TARGET workspace. | | ` bundle ` | required | The full envelope exactly as returned by export_loop_template. | | ` dry_run ` | optional | Defaults to true: report action, findings and diff_summary, and write nothing. Set false to apply. | ### Gotchas - `dry_run` defaults to TRUE — nothing is written until you re-call with dry_run=false, which adds template_id. - A commit always lands UNPUBLISHED, so an import can never change what a running board executes; publish_loop_template stays a separate act. - A matching slug in the target makes this action=updated — the existing DRAFT is overwritten. Check diff_summary in the dry run first. - Runner callers are refused with 403 by design: a runner must not import the prompt that governs it. Envelope mismatch → 400; unrenderable template → 422. - Bundles over ~64 KB are better sent to POST /loop-templates/import directly — large JSON bodies through MCP have been seen to garble. > [!DANGER] > Danger zone > > > > With dry_run=false a slug collision OVERWRITES the target workspace's existing draft for that slug. Export a backup bundle from the target first. ### Example prompt ``` Import this loop template bundle into <workspace> with import_loop_template. Dry run first, show me the diff_summary and any findings, and only apply after I confirm. ``` ### Related tools [export_loop_template](#tool-export_loop_template) [publish_loop_template](#tool-publish_loop_template) [list_loop_templates](#tool-list_loop_templates) <a id="tool-list_skills"></a> ## list_skills readRead-onlyIdempotentIn default hand ` mcp__valaris__list_skills ` List the workspace skill library, or a board's effective skill set, with each skill's declared toolsets. Metadata only — file contents live behind get_skill. ### What the model sees ``` List workspace skills, or a board's effective skill set with board_id. Metadata only (incl. each skill's declared toolsets and, for a board, the toolsets its loop grant does not cover); get_skill returns the files. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | optional | Board UUID or slug (backend-resolved). When given, returns the board's effective skill set instead of the full workspace library. | | ` include_archived ` | optional | Workspace listings hide archived skills by default; pass true to include them. Ignored when board_id is given. | ### Gotchas - Listings never inline file contents — install a skill by calling get_skill and writing each returned file verbatim into your local skills dir. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, list the skills available on the <board> board in <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [get_skill](#tool-get_skill) [set_skill_binding](#tool-set_skill_binding) <a id="tool-get_skill"></a> ## get_skill readRead-onlyIdempotentIn default hand ` mcp__valaris__get_skill ` Fetch a skill version's files verbatim (SKILL.md plus support files) and its declared toolsets. Omitting version resolves the latest published one. ### What the model sees ``` Fetch a skill version's files verbatim (with its declared toolsets). Long files are truncated; re-fetch one whole with file_path. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` slug ` | required | The skill slug. | | ` version ` | optional | Explicit version number. Omit to fetch the latest published version; pass explicitly to fetch a specific version or a draft. | | ` file_path ` | optional | Path of a single file to return in full, bypassing the per-file truncation cap. | ### Gotchas - Files longer than 6000 chars are truncated in the multi-file response (flagged via _files_truncated) — re-fetch each one in full with file_path. - A skill with no published version returns empty files; pass version explicitly to read a draft. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, fetch the pdf-tools skill from <workspace> and install its files locally. ``` ### Related tools [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) [set_skill_binding](#tool-set_skill_binding) <a id="tool-propose_skill"></a> ## propose_skill write ` mcp__valaris__propose_skill ` Propose a new skill (or version) for the workspace library. Lands as a draft pending human approval; idempotent — re-proposing returns the existing pending proposal. ### What the model sees ``` Propose a new skill or version as a draft pending human approval; nothing is served until approved. Idempotent: returns the pending proposal. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` slug ` | required | The skill slug the proposal creates or versions. | | ` files ` | required | The skill's files as [{"path": ..., "content": ...}] — SKILL.md plus any support files, contents sent verbatim. | | ` name ` | optional | Display name. Omit to let the backend take it from the SKILL.md frontmatter, which is authoritative. | | ` description ` | optional | Description. Omit to let the backend take it from the SKILL.md frontmatter, which is authoritative. | | ` board_id ` | optional | Board UUID or slug (backend-resolved) to associate the proposal with — e.g. the board whose loop produced it. | ### Gotchas - Nothing is published until a human approves — poll get_approval_status with the returned approval_id before relying on the skill. - File contents are sent verbatim on this write path — the 6000-char truncation cap only applies to reads via get_skill. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, propose a pdf-tools skill for <workspace> from the files in my local skills directory. ``` ### Related tools [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) [get_skill](#tool-get_skill) [get_approval_status](#tool-get_approval_status) <a id="tool-set_skill_binding"></a> ## set_skill_binding writeIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__set_skill_binding ` Enable or disable a workspace skill on a board, optionally pinning a version. Idempotent — re-binding updates in place. ### What the model sees ``` Upsert a skill binding on a board: enable/disable, optionally pin a version. Omitted fields are unchanged (tri-state); new bindings default to enabled, unpinned. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | The board UUID or slug (backend-resolved). | | ` skill_slug ` | required | The slug of the workspace skill to bind. | | ` enabled ` | optional | Whether the skill is active on the board. Omit to leave an existing binding's state unchanged; a newly created binding defaults to enabled. | | ` pinned_version ` | optional | Version number to pin the board to. Omit to leave any existing pin unchanged; an unpinned board tracks the latest published version. | | ` clear_pin ` | optional | Pass true to remove an existing version pin, returning the board to tracking the latest published version. Mutually exclusive with pinned_version. | ### Gotchas - Omitting pinned_version leaves an existing pin as-is (PUT semantics of an omitted field) — it does not clear the pin; unpin with clear_pin: true. - pinned_version and clear_pin together is an error — pin or unpin, not both. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, enable the pdf-tools skill on the <board> board in <workspace>, pinned to version 2. ``` ### Related tools [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) [get_skill](#tool-get_skill) [next_assignment](#tool-next_assignment) <a id="tool-list_skill_bindings_raw"></a> ## list_skill_bindings_raw readRead-onlyIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__list_skill_bindings_raw ` Raw view of a board's skill binding rows, disabled ones included. list_skills(board_id) is the effective set callers actually get. ### What the model sees ``` Raw view of a board's skill binding rows, disabled ones included; list_skills(board_id) is the effective set callers actually get. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | The board UUID or slug (backend-resolved). | ### Gotchas - Rows are configuration, not what agents get: a disabled binding or one resolving to no published version appears here but never in the board's effective set (list_skills with board_id). ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, call list_skill_bindings_raw on the <board> board in <workspace> to show every configured skill binding, including disabled ones. ``` ### Related tools [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) [set_skill_binding](#tool-set_skill_binding) [remove_skill_binding](#tool-remove_skill_binding) <a id="tool-remove_skill_binding"></a> ## remove_skill_binding writeDestructiveIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__remove_skill_binding ` Unbind a skill from a board, deleting the binding row (enabled flag and pin included). Idempotent — removing a missing binding still succeeds. ### What the model sees ``` Delete a board's skill binding row, pin included; disable via set_skill_binding to keep it. Idempotent. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` board_id ` | required | The board UUID or slug (backend-resolved). | | ` skill_slug ` | required | The slug of the bound skill to remove. | ### Gotchas - Unbind destroys the row's configuration — any version pin is lost. To keep the pin but take the skill out of the effective set, disable it instead via set_skill_binding with enabled: false. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, unbind the pdf-tools skill from the <board> board in <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [set_skill_binding](#tool-set_skill_binding) [list_skill_bindings_raw](#tool-list_skill_bindings_raw) <a id="tool-list_skill_catalog"></a> ## list_skill_catalog readRead-onlyIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__list_skill_catalog ` List the built-in skill catalog: platform-curated skills not yet in the workspace library, each with its declared toolsets, ready to activate. ### What the model sees ``` List the built-in skill catalog: curated bundles (each declaring the toolsets it plays in) not yet in the workspace library. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | ### Gotchas - Catalog entries are not workspace skills yet — activate one (activate_catalog_skill) to copy it into the library before it can be bound to boards. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, list the built-in skill catalog for <workspace>. ``` ### Related tools [activate_catalog_skill](#tool-activate_catalog_skill) [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) <a id="tool-activate_catalog_skill"></a> ## activate_catalog_skill writeIdempotent ` mcp__valaris__activate_catalog_skill ` Copy a catalog entry into the workspace library as a published v1. Idempotent — re-activation returns the existing copy untouched. ### What the model sees ``` Copy a catalog skill into the workspace library as published v1. Human sessions only (runner keys 403). Idempotent. ``` ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | The URL slug identifying the workspace. | | ` catalog_id ` | required | The catalog entry id, from list_skill_catalog. | ### Gotchas - Human sessions only: the backend rejects runner-bound callers (API keys linked to a runner identity) with a 403 — activation is a curation decision reserved for people. ### Example prompt ``` Using the Backplane MCP, activate the tdd-discipline catalog skill into <workspace> and bind it to the <board> board. ``` ### Related tools [list_skill_catalog](#tool-list_skill_catalog) [set_skill_binding](#tool-set_skill_binding) [list_skills](#tool-list_skills) <a id="prompt-init_project"></a> ## init_project Initializer Bootstrap a complete project from a raw brief: board, columns, definition, channels, seed cards, a pinned decision-log note, and git repo. Team members named in the brief are added as workspace members — that grants them workspace access. Use once when starting a new project in a workspace. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace the new board will live in. | | ` project_brief ` | required | Free-text brief: goals, tech stack, constraints, timeline, team, and repos — everything the agent should extract and scaffold from. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the Backplane init_project prompt for the <workspace> workspace with this brief: <paste your project brief>. Build the board end to end and show me the final verification summary. ``` <a id="prompt-standup"></a> ## standup Secretary Generate a daily standup for one board — progress, stale and overdue cards, bottlenecks — saved as a board note. Run each morning or before a team sync. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board to report on. | ### Example prompt ``` Run the standup prompt for board <board_id> in the <workspace> workspace. Post the report as a board note, but don't touch any cards unless I say so. ``` <a id="prompt-triage"></a> ## triage Secretary Audit board hygiene — missing priorities, empty descriptions, overdue or stale cards — into a health score with proposed fixes. Fixes run only after you confirm. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board to health-check. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the triage prompt on board <board_id> in the <workspace> workspace. Show me the health score and the issue list, then wait for my go-ahead before fixing anything. ``` <a id="prompt-status"></a> ## status Secretary Summarize every board in a workspace: completion, urgent and overdue counts, stalled boards, plus the top 3 recommended actions. Use for a weekly or executive overview. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace to summarize across all of its boards. | ### Example prompt ``` Run the status prompt for the <workspace> workspace and give me the cross-board health table plus your top three recommended actions. ``` <a id="prompt-plan_work"></a> ## plan_work Architect Decompose a high-level objective into sequenced backlog cards (1-3 days each) gated by an ACCEPT- acceptance card. Use when planning a new feature or chunk of work. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board where the cards will be created. | | ` objective ` | required | The high-level objective to break down into cards. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the plan_work prompt on board <board_id> in <workspace> with the objective: <objective>. Show me the sequenced plan before creating any cards. ``` <a id="prompt-decompose_card"></a> ## decompose_card Architect Split one oversized card into smaller, independently deliverable child cards that inherit its labels and priority. Use when a card is too big for 1-3 days of work. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board the card lives on. | | ` card_id ` | required | ID of the oversized card to split. | ### Example prompt ``` Run decompose_card on card <card_id> (board <board_id>, workspace <workspace>). Propose the split first, and don't delete the parent card without asking me. ``` <a id="prompt-sprint"></a> ## sprint Architect Plan a sprint: measure velocity, select backlog cards within capacity, stage them in the sprint column with due dates and owners, and pin a sprint-plan note. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board to plan the sprint on. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the sprint prompt for board <board_id> in <workspace>. Show me the selected-cards table before moving anything, then document the plan as a pinned note. ``` <a id="prompt-pickup"></a> ## pickup Coder Claim a card interactively: pick from the backlog-typed column, move it into the active-typed column, and output an implementation brief. Runners use next_assignment. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board to pick up work from. | | ` card_id ` | optional | Card to pick up. Omit to auto-select the highest-priority unassigned card in the backlog-typed column (resolved by column_type, never by column name). If no column on the board has a column_type, the prompt first types the columns via update_column rather than guessing by name. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the pickup prompt on board <board_id> in <workspace> — pick the best available card for me, claim it by moving it into the working column, and give me the implementation brief. ``` <a id="prompt-implement"></a> ## implement Coder Run the full delivery loop for one card: claim it, plan against the codebase, implement with strict TDD, verify, then move it to review with an implementation record. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board the card lives on. | | ` card_id ` | required | ID of the card to implement. | ### Example prompt ``` Run the implement prompt for card <card_id> on board <board_id> in <workspace>. Follow the TDD loop and show me your implementation plan before writing code. ``` <a id="prompt-ship"></a> ## ship Coder Close out a reviewed card: move it to Done, mark it completed, write a completion note, report newly unblocked cards, and suggest the next card to pick up. ### Parameters | Name | Required | Description | | --- | --- | --- | | ` workspace_slug ` | required | Slug of the workspace that owns the board. | | ` board_id ` | required | ID of the board the card lives on. | | ` card_id ` | required | ID of the reviewed card to complete. | ### Example prompt ``` Use the ship prompt for card <card_id> on board <board_id> in <workspace>. Complete it, record the completion note, and tell me what it unblocked and what to pick up next. ``` <a id="resource-valaris://workspaces"></a> ## valaris://workspaces List of all workspaces you can access, with slugs and metadata. Read this first to discover the workspace_slug that every other call needs. <a id="resource-valaris://workspace/{workspace_slug}/summary"></a> ## valaris://workspace/{workspace_slug}/summary Aggregate stats for one workspace: board, card, note, and channel counts plus recent activity. Same data as the get_workspace_summary tool. <a id="resource-valaris://workspace/{workspace_slug}/board/{board_id}/definition"></a> ## valaris://workspace/{workspace_slug}/board/{board_id}/definition The board's definition document: scope plus structured content (objectives, tech stack, milestones, constraints). Same data as the get_definition tool.

en.title: MCP Toolsets
en.markdown: MCP Reference # MCP Toolsets A toolset is a named slice of the MCP surface. Every group and every category of the tool catalog is one, addressed by its id, and the server lists and serves only the tools in the toolsets you load. A tool that is not listed cannot be called either, so the model never sees a name it may not use. A [skill](../documentation/skills) declares the toolsets its playbook plays in; that declaration is guidance, and only the loaded toolsets enforce. ## The env contract ` VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS ` is read once when the MCP server starts. Unset or empty it means ` default `, the interactive hand described below. ` all ` loads every tool. Anything else is a comma-separated list of toolset ids; ` default ` may appear in that list and expands to the default hand. Ids are case-sensitive and whitespace around the commas is ignored. > [!IMPORTANT] > Unknown ids fail closed > > > > An id that is not a group id, a category id, ` all `, or ` default ` stops the server at startup with an error naming the offending ids and the valid ones. A typo never silently disables the gate. ## The default hand Unless told otherwise the server serves the interactive default hand: the union of these group toolsets minus a short exclusion list, plus a short inclusion list of read-only helpers from the other groups. It currently resolves to 57 tools. Groups in the default hand: ` start-here `, ` work-management `, ` knowledge-content ` Excluded from it, even though their group is loaded: | Tool | Why it is excluded | | --- | --- | | ` add_workspace_member ` | workspace admin, pairs with remove_workspace_member | | ` delete_board ` | destroys a board and every card on it | | ` delete_column ` | cascade-deletes every card in the column | | ` delete_workspace ` | destroys the whole workspace | | ` freeze_board ` | workspace admin | | ` next_assignment ` | runner-only pickup path; interactive sessions claim by move_card | | ` remove_workspace_member ` | workspace admin | | ` unfreeze_board ` | workspace admin, pairs with freeze_board | | ` update_workspace_member ` | workspace admin, pairs with remove_workspace_member | Pulled into it from groups the default hand does not load: | Tool | Why it is included | | --- | --- | | ` get_skill ` | the server instructions tell interactive agents to install the board's skills | | ` get_workspace_metrics ` | read-only reporting used by the standup workflow | | ` list_git_repos ` | read-only; boards are linked to repos | | ` list_skills ` | the server instructions tell interactive agents to install the board's skills | The other groups are opt-in: ` collaboration `, ` autonomous-operations `. Add them to the list when the session needs workspace setup or runner administration. ## Available toolsets One row per toolset. no toolset lists them. Presets are starting selections. Preserve custom toolset compositions and existing credentials. Actual autonomous runner launches use all intersected with their authorized allowlist; do not replace that execution configuration with the interactive loops preset. - ` all ` loads every tool. This is what runner launches pin. - ` default ` loads the interactive hand, the same as leaving the variable unset. - ` default,autonomous-operations ` loads the interactive hand plus one whole opt-in group. - ` cards,notes ` loads just those two categories, for a session that only edits cards and notes. ## Composition with the allowlist ` VALARIS_MCP_ALLOWLIST ` and ` VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS ` are independent gates, and the served hand is their intersection: a tool must be in a loaded toolset and, when an allowlist is set, on that allowlist to be listed or called. Neither variable can widen what the other narrowed. Runners pin ` all `. The stage allowlist a runner receives from the backend is meant to be the only narrowing, so the runner's generated MCP config always sets ` VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS ` to ` all `; a default-hand template would clip a stage grant twice. ## Discovery from inside a session ` get_server_info ` reports which toolsets are loaded, how many tools resolved, what the default hand is, every id that exists, and a hint on how to widen the hand. A denied call to a tool outside the loaded toolsets names the loaded ids in its error, so the model can ask for a wider hand instead of guessing. ` VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS ` picks the initial hand; ` enable_toolsets ` widens a running session by adding toolsets, and the server then sends ` tools/list_changed ` to request a client refresh; delivery does not prove the agent received new tools. Widening is one-way and not persisted. If tools remain absent, use the returned restart_env in the MCP server startup configuration, restart the server/connection and start a new agent session. For remote HTTP, the server operator must update that environment. Keep the runner allowlist unchanged. Use the exact returned restart_env for recovery: it preserves every enabled group, including custom toolsets. Keep existing credentials and VALARIS_MCP_ALLOWLIST unchanged. The following fresh connection example is for interactive loops; it must not replace a wider recovered selection. bash Remote MCP service startup environment ```bash MCP_TRANSPORT=streamable-http MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0 VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS=default,autonomous-operations ``` The remote operator applies these values to the actual MCP service startup environment, retains the existing API/authentication configuration, and protects the endpoint behind authenticated access or a trusted private network. MCP_HOST=0.0.0.0 is a bind address, not access control. Local client environment cannot change a remote service. Restart the MCP server/connection, then start a fresh agent session and repeat the read-only native checks. A new chat alone may reuse a stale server or cached catalog. Repeating enable_toolsets cannot force a client refresh. If a tool is still missing, check the running version, startup toolsets and authorized allowlist before changing configuration.

en.title: MCP Prompt Catalog
en.markdown: Reference # MCP Prompt Catalog Prompts are server-authored multi-phase workflow templates. An MCP host (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, a runner) expands a prompt by name and gets back a long instruction block that the LLM then executes as a sequenced plan. The templates do not share one universal phase cadence or confirmation rule: ` triage ` explicitly waits for confirmation before applying fixes, while ` decompose_card ` asks before deleting a parent card. Other prompts can present a plan and then proceed without a second confirmation gate. 10 prompts total, organized by agent role. Parameters are interpolated into the prompt body at expansion time. The LLM sees the rendered string; parameter names are not visible to it. Invoking a prompt is not a transaction boundary: the host sends rendered prose to the model, and any resulting tool calls still run through normal authentication, authorization, and MCP allowlist checks. ## The prompts | Prompt | Role | Parameters | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ` init_project ` | Initializer | ` workspace_slug, project_brief ` | Bootstrap a complete project from a raw brief: board, columns, definition, channels, seed cards, a pinned decision-log note, and git repo. Team members named in the brief are added as workspace members — that grants them workspace access. Use once when starting a new project in a workspace. | | ` standup ` | Secretary | ` workspace_slug, board_id ` | Generate a daily standup for one board — progress, stale and overdue cards, bottlenecks — saved as a board note. Run each morning or before a team sync. | | ` triage ` | Secretary | ` workspace_slug, board_id ` | Audit board hygiene — missing priorities, empty descriptions, overdue or stale cards — into a health score with proposed fixes. Fixes run only after you confirm. | | ` status ` | Secretary | ` workspace_slug ` | Summarize every board in a workspace: completion, urgent and overdue counts, stalled boards, plus the top 3 recommended actions. Use for a weekly or executive overview. | | ` plan_work ` | Architect | ` workspace_slug, board_id, objective ` | Decompose a high-level objective into sequenced backlog cards (1-3 days each) gated by an ACCEPT- acceptance card. Use when planning a new feature or chunk of work. | | ` decompose_card ` | Architect | ` workspace_slug, board_id, card_id ` | Split one oversized card into smaller, independently deliverable child cards that inherit its labels and priority. Use when a card is too big for 1-3 days of work. | | ` sprint ` | Architect | ` workspace_slug, board_id ` | Plan a sprint: measure velocity, select backlog cards within capacity, stage them in the sprint column with due dates and owners, and pin a sprint-plan note. | | ` pickup ` | Coder | ` workspace_slug, board_id, card_id? ` | Claim a card interactively: pick from the backlog-typed column, move it into the active-typed column, and output an implementation brief. Runners use next_assignment. | | ` implement ` | Coder | ` workspace_slug, board_id, card_id ` | Run the full delivery loop for one card: claim it, plan against the codebase, implement with strict TDD, verify, then move it to review with an implementation record. | | ` ship ` | Coder | ` workspace_slug, board_id, card_id ` | Close out a reviewed card: move it to Done, mark it completed, write a completion note, report newly unblocked cards, and suggest the next card to pick up. | ## How a host invokes them In Claude Code and Claude Desktop, prompts appear in the slash- command palette. The host fetches the prompt template, interpolates any parameters the user typed, and sends the resulting prose to the model as a user turn. The model then executes it as a plan — no different from the user typing a long, careful instruction by hand. The Go runner does not expand this MCP prompt catalog during stage assembly. It fetches workspace prompt configurations and pipeline assignments through REST, then gives the spawned coding-agent session its allowed MCP tools. MCP prompts are host-facing templates, separate from the platform's pipeline prompt configurations. > [!HONEST] > The slash-command name and the MCP handle disagree > > > > The MCP install guide's workflow overview shows prompts with dashed names — ` /init-project `, ` /plan-work `, ` /decompose `. The MCP server registers them with underscores — ` init_project `, ` plan_work `, ` decompose_card `. A user typing the dashed form into a host that strictly matches registered MCP names will come up empty. Use the underscore handles shown in this catalog; dashed aliases are not registered by the server.

en.title: Event Taxonomy
en.markdown: Reference # Event Taxonomy Every relevant mutation publishes through the event-bus interface selected by ` EVENT_BUS_BACKEND `. ` memory ` delivers only to subscribers in the same process; ` postgres ` preserves that local fan-out and adds cross-instance delivery through Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY. Both feed WebSocket connections and the origin instance's external-webhook subscriber. Events carry a ` workspace_id ` and a ` payload `; subscribers filter by ` fnmatch ` pattern (` activity.card.* `, ` activity.*.deleted `, ` * `). The authoritative surface is the ` activity.* ` namespace —` ActivityService.record ` emits one of these for every entity mutation it records. The other namespaces carry events the activity fan-out doesn't cover: approvals, executions, runner lifecycle, config changes, cost alerts. ## activity.* — primary fan-out Emitted as ` activity.{entity_type}.{action} `. The payload matches the activity-log row (entity_id, action, actor_id, optional board_id, summary, changes). | Namespace | Actions emitted | | --- | --- | | ` activity.card.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` moved `, ` deleted `, ` dependency_added `, ` dependency_removed `, ` dependencies_replaced ` | | ` activity.column.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.board.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.note.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.resource.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.definition.* ` | ` created `, ` updated ` | | ` activity.channel.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.git_repo.* ` | ` created `, ` updated `, ` deleted ` | | ` activity.workspace.* ` | ` created `, ` updated ` | | ` activity.member.* ` | ` added_member `, ` removed_member ` | | ` activity.agent.* ` | ` updated `, ` deleted ` — lifecycle detail is carried in ` changes.lifecycle ` | ## Service-owned event namespaces Events published directly by their owning services — not activity rows. These carry service-specific payload shapes. | Event | Publisher | Key payload fields | | --- | --- | --- | | ` approval.created ` | ` ApprovalService.create_approval ` | ` approval_id, status, category, risk_score, action_description, agent_id ` | | ` approval.updated ` | ` ApprovalService.decide ` | ` approval_id, status, decided_by, decision_reason ` | | ` execution.started ` | ` ExecutionService.start_execution ` | ` execution_id, agent_id, action, input_summary, board_id ` | | ` execution.completed ` | ` ExecutionService.update_execution ` (terminal status) | ` execution_id, status, cost_usd, tokens_used, output_summary, error_message ` | | ` execution.warning ` | ` ExecutionService.record_warning ` | ` execution_id, agent_id, card_id, board_id, kind, message `; an in-flight warning, not completion | | ` agent.status_changed ` | ` AgentService ` on activate / deactivate / re- activate | ` agent_id, is_active, previous_active ` | | ` agent.poll_requested ` | ` AgentService.poll_agent ` (WS-gated; 503 without an active connection) | ` target_agent_id ` | | ` agent.heartbeat_received ` | ` AgentService.handle_ws_heartbeat ` | ` agent_id, status, last_seen_at, liveness ` | | ` agent.paused `, ` agent.resumed ` | ` AgentService.pause_agent / resume_agent ` | ` agent_id, is_paused ` | | ` agent.restart_requested `, ` agent.hard_deleted ` | ` AgentService.restart_agent / hard_delete_agent ` | ` target_agent_id ` for restart; ` agent_id ` for deletion | | ` board.loop_updated ` | ` BoardService ` after a loop-state change | ` workspace_id, board_id, enabled, version, disabled_reason ` | | ` api_key.first_used ` | ` ApiKeyService ` on the key's first-ever use | ` api_key_id, user_id, key_name, last_used_at `; WebSocket delivery is restricted to that user | | ` notification.created ` | In-app notification channel, after the outer transaction commits | ` notification_id, recipient_user_id, category, workspace_id, unread_delta, link `; WebSocket delivery is restricted to the recipient | | ` merge_queue.enqueued ` through ` merge_queue.ci_not_green ` | ` MergeQueueService ` | ` entry_id, card_id, repo_id, integration_branch, pr_url, pr_branch, state, attempt_count `, plus outcome fields | | ` merge_queue.stale ` | ` BoardHealthService ` on the first stale detection | Queue identity plus ` board_id, age_seconds, classification `; latched to emit once per entry | | ` merge_queue.conflict_consolidator_created ` | ` ConsolidatorCardCreator ` | ` entry_id, original_card_id, consolidator_card_id ` | | ` board.loop_updated ` | ` BoardService ` on loop config save, enable / disable, and loop-template bind / re-render / detach | ` workspace_id, board_id, enabled, version, disabled_reason ` — deliberately thin (the NOTIFY payload cap); clients refetch rather than read state off the event | | ` config.changed ` | Agent / team / prompt_config / workspace_config / loop_template services | ` entity, action, entity_id ` — plus ` slug, version ` when ` entity = loop_template `, whose actions extend beyond created/updated/deleted to ` published, archived, unarchived, restored ` | | ` cost.threshold_crossed ` | ` AlertThresholdService ` | ` threshold_id, metric, operator, target_value, current_value, workspace_id, board_id ` | ## Deprecated — bridge events (still firing) Before the ` activity.* ` fan-out existed, the platform emitted un-namespaced lifecycle events directly. A small number of these still publish in parallel with their ` activity.* ` twin so pre-migration subscribers don't break. New code should not subscribe to these. | Event | Replacement | | --- | --- | | ` card.created `, ` card.updated `, ` card.moved `, ` card.deleted ` | ` activity.card.{action} ` | | ` column.created `, ` column.updated `, ` column.deleted ` | ` activity.column.{action} ` | ## Delivery boundaries The live EventBus and WebSocket surface is broader than the public webhook selector. The ` WebhookEvent ` schema currently exposes the bridge events, the listed ` activity.* ` pairs through ` activity.member.* `, and the original approval, execution, agent-status, config, and cost events. It does not expose ` activity.agent.* ` or the newer direct events such as ` execution.warning `, ` agent.paused `, ` agent.resumed `, ` agent.restart_requested `, ` agent.hard_deleted `, ` board.loop_updated `, ` api_key.first_used `, ` notification.created `, or ` merge_queue.* `. Those names cannot be selected through the webhook create or update API today. Two additional names, ` agent.restart_probe ` and ` agent.restart_ack `, coordinate restart discovery between backend workers. The connection manager explicitly suppresses them from client WebSockets. ` notification.created ` and ` api_key.first_used ` are also filtered per user rather than broadcast to every workspace member. > [!HONEST] > A live notification bus is not an audit log > > > > Both backends provide at-most-once delivery with no replay. The memory backend also stops at the process boundary; Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY closes that visibility gap but is still not a durable queue. Use the persisted activity, execution, approval, notification, and merge-queue rows as the source of truth, and treat events as prompts to refetch.

en.title: Column Type Semantics
en.markdown: Reference # Column Type Semantics A column has two identities. Its **name** is what humans read on the board. Its ` column_type ` is what pipelines and runners match against. Rename a column and nothing else changes. Retype a column and you've rewired part of the pipeline. Five types exist today. The set is closed — operators can't declare new column types the way they can declare new roles. A column can also be untyped (` null `), in which case pipeline stages with a ` by_column_type ` discover strategy will simply not see it. ## The types | column_type | Semantic meaning | Typical pipeline stages that target it | | --- | --- | --- | | ` backlog ` | Unstarted work. Usually unassigned, sometimes untriaged. The source of truth for "what could be done next." | Architect stages (` plan_work `, ` sprint `), triage, decomposition. | | ` active ` | In-progress work. A runner has claimed a card here (or will). Also the destination of "start work" transitions. | Implementer stages (` implement `, ` implement_after_approval `), pickup. | | ` review ` | Work awaiting evaluation. A reviewer role looks here for cards to pull and verdict on. | Reviewer stages, rework mediation, documentator walks. | | ` done ` | Terminal success. Cards land here after a ship. Documentator stages often sweep this column for post-merge notes. | Documentator, post-ship hooks. | | ` blocked ` | Work that can't progress — missing dependency, external wait, failed sensor. Rarely a destination; usually where a stage moves a card when ` on_failure ` fires. | Failure paths, sensor rejections, manual operator moves. | > [!IMPORTANT] > The type is the contract, the name is cosmetic > > > > Pipeline ` discover ` strategies and ` on_success ` / ` on_failure ` actions reference ` column_type `, never ` column_name `. A column named "Peer Review" with type ` review ` and a column named "Review" with type ` review ` are indistinguishable to a pipeline stage. Two columns sharing a type is supported — stages match all of them. A column with no type (` null `) is invisible to type-matching stages. ## Practical consequences - You can have multiple ` backlog ` columns (e.g., "Ideas" and "Next Sprint") and a single architect stage will treat them as one pool. - Renaming "Done" to "Shipped" changes what the board looks like, not what the documentator stage discovers. - Dropping a column's type to ` null ` removes it from pipeline scope without deleting its cards — useful for staging a column out of rotation. - Adding a new column-type value is a backend change (enum + migration), not a configuration change. The current five cover the kanban idioms we've needed.

en.title: Card Type and Priority
en.markdown: Reference # Card Type and Priority Two enums on every card affect both visual styling on the board and the order in which discover strategies offer cards to runners. They are cosmetic in isolation and load-bearing in combination — ` priority ` in particular drives which card a polling runner sees first. ## Card type Four values. Each maps to a Tailwind token in ` KanbanCard.tsx ` — no hex strings in the source. Type does not affect pipeline matching unless a stage filter explicitly references it; it's primarily a visual and human-filter concern. | card_type | Visual | Intended use | | --- | --- | --- | | ` task ` | Neutral token — the default. | The generic unit of work. Anything not obviously a bug, a new feature, or an open issue. | | ` bug ` | Rose / red-accented token. | Regression, defect, broken behavior. Pipelines that run a reproduction-first TDD flow typically filter to this type. | | ` feature ` | Emerald / green-accented token. | New capability. Usually decomposed by an architect stage before an implementer claims it. | | ` issue ` | Amber-accented token. | Open question, investigation, ambiguous report. Promoted to` bug ` or ` feature ` once triaged. | ## Priority Five values, ordered. The ordering matters: discover strategies that return "highest priority first" use this enum as their sort key. Ties break on fractional position within the column, so priority acts as the primary key and position acts as the secondary. The API schema and the ` create_card ` MCP tool default to ` none `. The create-card dialog defaults to medium and does not currently offer none in its selector, although existing ` none ` cards render correctly elsewhere in the UI. Callers that need an explicit unset priority should use the API or MCP surface. | priority | Rank | Discover implication | | --- | --- | --- | | ` urgent ` | Highest | Pulled first by priority-ordered discover. Runners will claim an ` urgent ` card in ` backlog ` before touching a ` high ` card in the same column. | | ` high ` | High | Second wave. The default for non-trivial work an architect stage creates via ` plan_work `. | | ` medium ` | Medium (create-dialog default) | The browser's create-card dialog preselects this value. API and MCP callers that omit priority create a ` none ` card instead. | | ` low ` | Low | Pulled after medium but before unprioritized ` none `. Useful for nice-to-haves when the runner has spare capacity. | | ` none ` | Unprioritized (API and MCP default) | Sorted after ` low `. Use this value when priority has not been triaged yet; it is not selectable in the current create-card dialog. | ## Combined effect A ` by_priority ` discover strategy sorts ` urgent ` → ` high ` → ` medium ` → ` low ` → ` none `, then by fractional position within each bucket. A human dragging a card to the top of a column is effectively saying "same priority, try me first"; an operator bumping priority is saying "jump the line across buckets." Both paths reach the same runner; the runner doesn't know or care which one put the card on top.

en.title: API Authentication Modes
en.markdown: Reference # API Authentication Modes The backend accepts several auth modes, evaluated in a fixed order: API key, then the signed session cookie (in production), then dev mode (in development), then IAP, then trusted proxy. Whichever signal arrives first wins. This lets a single codebase serve dev laptops, self-hosted boxes with the built-in password login, OIDC or IAP-gated production, and API-key-bearing runners without branching logic at every router. On the proxy-verified tiers (IAP, trusted proxy) users are auto-provisioned on first authenticated request (unless ` AUTH_AUTO_PROVISION=false `). OIDC applies the same provisioning policy during its callback. With local password login, accounts come from the first-run setup screen or from a workspace admin — there is no self-registration. ## The modes | Mode | When used | Header(s) expected | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **API key** | Runners, MCP callers, server-to-server integrations. Preferred for any automated caller. | ` Authorization: Bearer vlr_... ` | Backend matches the key by prefix + hash. The prefix column is stored; the full key is hashed at rest and shown to the user exactly once at creation time. | | **Dev mode** | Local development only. Active when ` ENV=development ` and no bearer token is present. | ` X-User-Email: you@example.com ` | Falls back to ` dev@valaris.dev ` if the header is absent. This fallback is disabled outside development. | | **Local password** | Browser traffic on self-hosted instances with no identity provider. On by default (` LOCAL_AUTH_ENABLED=true `); needs ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` to mint sessions. | ` Cookie: backplane_session= ` | ` POST /api/auth/login ` verifies an argon2id-hashed password and mints the same signed session cookie as OIDC — the cookie tier does not care how identity was proven. Every failed login is one uniform 401; attempts are throttled per IP and 5 straight failures lock the account for 15 minutes. See [local password login](#local-login) below. | | **OIDC session** | Browser traffic when you point Backplane at your own identity provider. The login affordance is active only when ` OIDC_ISSUER `, ` OIDC_CLIENT_ID `, and ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` are all set. | ` Cookie: backplane_session= ` | Minted by ` /api/auth/oidc/callback ` after an authorization-code + PKCE login. Signed with ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY `, httponly, and valid for ` OIDC_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS `. Outranks IAP and trusted proxy; an invalid cookie is a rejection, never a fallback to a weaker tier. | | **IAP (JWT)** | Production browser traffic behind Google IAP. Active when ` IAP_AUDIENCE ` is set. | ` X-Goog-IAP-JWT-Assertion: ` | Backend verifies the JWT against Google's public keys with ` google.oauth2.id_token.verify_token ` and extracts the email claim. A missing or invalid JWT is a 403, not a fallback. | | **Trusted proxy (header)** | Production behind an authenticating proxy (IAP, oauth2-proxy, Authelia). Opt-in: set ` TRUSTED_PROXY_AUTH=true `. Never automatic. | ` : you@example.com ` | No signature to verify, so the header is trusted only because the proxy is the only thing that can set it. Safe only when the backend is unreachable except through that proxy and the proxy strips client-supplied copies. Optionally set ` TRUSTED_PROXY_SECRET ` and have the proxy inject ` X-Backplane-Proxy-Secret ` — requests without the matching value are rejected even if they carry the identity header. With neither this nor ` IAP_AUDIENCE `, production refuses to start. | Two provisioning knobs apply to verified browser identities (IAP, trusted proxy, and OIDC), not to API keys or dev mode: ` AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS ` restricts sign-in to a comma-separated list of email domains, and ` AUTH_AUTO_PROVISION=false ` switches to invite-only. IAP and trusted-proxy requests receive HTTP 403 when the verified email has no existing account. The OIDC callback redirects with HTTP 302 to ` {FRONTEND_URL}/login?code=user_not_provisioned ` instead; it does not return a 403 page from the callback. Neither path creates a fresh user row. The domain allowlist also gates the local-auth paths that mint a login-capable account: first-run setup and an admin invite that grants an initial password (a plain, passwordless membership invite is a deliberate act and is not domain-checked). Rejections are logged with reason codes such as ` invalid_iap_jwt `, ` email_domain_not_allowed `, and ` user_not_provisioned ` so an auth outage is diagnosable from logs alone. ## Headers, by example http API key — runners and MCP callers ```http GET /api/workspaces/acme/boards HTTP/1.1 Host: valaris.example.com Authorization: Bearer vlr_9a2f...e1c0 Accept: application/json ``` http Dev mode — local laptop only ```http GET /api/workspaces/acme/boards HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8000 X-User-Email: dev@valaris.dev Accept: application/json ``` http IAP JWT — production browser traffic ```http GET /api/workspaces/acme/boards HTTP/1.1 Host: backplane.example.com X-Goog-IAP-JWT-Assertion: eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6I... Accept: application/json ``` ## Local password login A fresh instance with an empty ` users ` table serves a first-run setup screen: the first account created there becomes the instance's first user, and the setup route self-closes the moment any user exists (it reopens only if the table is ever empty again — an empty table means nobody can log in anyway). Passwords are stored as argon2id hashes with a 12-character minimum and no composition rules. Brute-force defence is two independent layers: a 10-requests-per-minute per-IP throttle on ` POST /api/auth/login `, and a DB-backed account lockout — 5 consecutive failures lock the account for 15 minutes. The lockout lives on the ` users ` row, so it holds across replicas and restarts, and it expires on its own. On the wire a locked account, a wrong password, and a nonexistent email are all the same 401; operators can tell them apart from log reason codes. Account management runs through workspace membership: a workspace **owner or admin** can add a member by email with an optional initial password (applied only if the account has no password yet), and can generate a temporary password for any member of that workspace — shown exactly once, and it clears an active lockout. That temporary password is the recovery path: there is no SMTP dependency and no email-based reset. Everyone can change their own password from the sidebar, which requires the current password. > [!DANGER] > Anyone who manages a workspace can create accounts > > > > Instance-level authority is deliberately derived from workspace roles — there is no separate admin flag. The corollary: on an instance with several workspaces owned by different people, each of those owners (and their admins) can create instance-wide accounts and set temporary passwords for their own members. If that is too broad for your deployment, keep workspace ownership narrow. Two more honest notes: changing a password does not invalidate sessions minted earlier (the cookie is stateless), and admin-set passwords are not flagged temporary — nothing forces a rotation on first login. ## Signing in with your own identity provider Set ` OIDC_ISSUER `, ` OIDC_CLIENT_ID `, and ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` and Backplane runs a backend-driven authorization-code flow with PKCE against any OpenID Connect provider (Keycloak, Authentik, Google, Entra, Okta). Everything else — authorization endpoint, token endpoint, JWKS, logout — is read from the issuer's discovery document, so there are no per-endpoint settings to drift out of sync. Tokens never reach the browser: the callback verifies the ID token server-side and mints a signed session cookie. Register ` {API_URL}/api/auth/oidc/callback ` as the redirect URI with your provider. ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` is required — without it no session can be signed, and the login button stays hidden. bash Keycloak — realm 'backplane' ```bash # Keycloak: Clients -> Create client # Client ID: backplane # Client authentication: On (confidential client) # Valid redirect URIs: https://backplane.example.com/api/auth/oidc/callback # Copy the generated secret from the Credentials tab. OIDC_ISSUER=https://keycloak.example.com/realms/backplane OIDC_CLIENT_ID=backplane OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET= OIDC_SCOPES=openid email profile OIDC_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS=43200 OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY= # Optional tenant boundary — an IdP proves identity, not membership: AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS=example.com ``` bash Google as the identity provider ```bash # Google Cloud console -> APIs & Services -> Credentials # Create OAuth client ID -> Web application # Authorized redirect URI: # https://backplane.example.com/api/auth/oidc/callback OIDC_ISSUER=https://accounts.google.com OIDC_CLIENT_ID=.apps.googleusercontent.com OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET= OIDC_SCOPES=openid email profile OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY= # Google will happily authenticate ANY Google account, so restrict the # domain unless you really mean "anyone with a Gmail address": AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS=example.com ``` > [!DANGER] > An identity provider proves identity, not membership > > > > Every mainstream IdP will authenticate accounts far outside your organization — Google signs in any Gmail user, and a Keycloak realm with self-registration enabled signs in anyone who fills the form. Unless ` AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS ` is set, any successful login auto-provisions a Backplane user. Set the domain allowlist, or run invite-only with ` AUTH_AUTO_PROVISION=false `. ## WebSocket auth The workspace WebSocket endpoint (` /ws/workspaces/{slug}/events `) accepts the same API key via ` Authorization ` on the upgrade request. Browser clients are authenticated by whatever authenticates their HTTP traffic — the session cookie (browsers send cookies on the handshake) or the IAP/proxy headers — so there is no extra browser step. A legacy ` ?token=vlr_... ` fallback is still accepted for API keys, but the Authorization header is preferred because query strings can land in access logs. > [!DANGER] > API key material is shown exactly once > > > > When an authenticated user creates an API key, the full ` vlr_... ` string is displayed once in the "API key created" dialog and never again. The backend stores only the prefix and a hash. If a key is lost, there is no recovery path — revoke it and mint a new one. Don't share keys over chat, don't commit them to repos, and don't bake them into runner config files that will be checked in. Treat a leaked key as an incident: revoke first, investigate second.

en.title: Environment Variables
en.markdown: Reference # Environment Variables Three processes read environment variables directly: the FastAPI backend, the MCP server, and the Go runner (` backplane-runner `). None of them require a full environment to start in dev mode — the defaults described below get you a working localhost. These tables cover the supported deployment, authentication, integration, event, MCP, and runner controls in the current code; one-off test variables are not part of this operator contract. ## Backend (FastAPI) Read from ` backend/app/config.py ` via ` pydantic-settings `. Values come from ` .env ` or the process environment; environment wins. | Variable | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | ` DATABASE_URL ` | ` postgresql+asyncpg://valaris:valaris@localhost:5433/valaris ` | Async SQLAlchemy DSN. Deployed environments point it at their Postgres instance. Must use the asyncpg driver. | | ` ENV ` | ` development ` | Gates dev-mode behaviors (swagger exposure, dev-mode auth fallback). Set to ` production ` in deployed environments. | | ` CORS_ORIGINS ` | ` http://localhost:5173 ` | Comma-separated allowlist. The frontend Cloud Run URL goes here in production. | | ` IAP_AUDIENCE ` | ` "" ` | Activates IAP JWT verification. Takes precedence over ` TRUSTED_PROXY_AUTH ` when both are set. Prod value is the full backend-service resource path. | | ` TRUSTED_PROXY_AUTH ` | ` false ` | Opt-in to trusting the identity header named by ` TRUSTED_PROXY_AUTH_HEADER ` (default ` X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email `; oauth2-proxy users set ` X-Forwarded-Email `). Only safe behind an authenticating proxy. | | ` TRUSTED_PROXY_SECRET ` | ` "" ` | Optional handshake for trusted-proxy mode: when set, requests must also carry ` X-Backplane-Proxy-Secret ` with this value. Configure the proxy to inject it. | | ` AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAIL_DOMAINS ` | ` "" ` | Comma-separated domains for verified IAP, trusted-proxy, and OIDC identities. It also gates local setup and admin-invite paths that create a password-capable account. Empty allows any verified domain; API keys and dev mode are exempt. | | ` AUTH_AUTO_PROVISION ` | ` true ` | Create user accounts on first verified sign-in. ` false ` makes the deployment invite-only: IAP and proxy requests for unknown users get 403, while the OIDC callback redirects with ` user_not_provisioned `. Neither creates a user row. | | ` LOCAL_AUTH_ENABLED ` | ` true ` | Enables database-backed email and password login. A production instance using local login also needs ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` to mint session cookies. | | ` OIDC_ISSUER ` | ` "" ` | OpenID Connect issuer URL. Empty disables OIDC; discovery supplies the authorization, token, JWKS, and logout endpoints. | | ` OIDC_CLIENT_ID ` | ` "" ` | Client identifier registered at the OIDC provider. OIDC is exposed to the browser only when this, ` OIDC_ISSUER `, and ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` are set. | | ` OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET ` | ` "" ` | Confidential-client secret sent during the authorization-code exchange. Keep it out of committed files. | | ` OIDC_SCOPES ` | ` openid email profile ` | Space-separated scopes requested from the identity provider. The verified ID token must supply an email claim. | | ` OIDC_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS ` | ` 43200 ` | Lifetime for signed browser sessions created by OIDC and local password login. Sessions are stateless and expire by age. | | ` OAUTH_STATE_SIGNING_KEY ` | ` "" ` | Signs login sessions plus OIDC and GitHub OAuth state. A production instance with local auth or OIDC enabled refuses to start when this is empty. | | ` FRONTEND_URL ` | ` http://localhost:5173 ` | Public browser origin used by login and integration redirects; its scheme also decides whether session cookies are Secure. | | ` EVENT_BUS_BACKEND ` | ` memory ` | Selects ` memory ` for single-process delivery or ` postgres ` for cross-instance delivery over Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY. ` redis ` is reserved but not implemented. | | ` CACHE_SINGLE_INSTANCE ` | ` false ` | Enables Tier-1 process caches. Safe on the memory bus only for a genuinely single-instance deployment; the Postgres bus distributes eviction events across instances. | | ` BACKPLANE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED ` | ` false ` | Opt-in anonymous instance telemetry. It sends nothing unless enabled and an endpoint is configured. | | ` BACKPLANE_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT ` | ` "" ` | Receiver for opt-in telemetry. Empty keeps telemetry a no-op even when the enable flag is true. | | ` API_URL ` | ` http://localhost:8000 ` | Operator-facing backend URL baked into exported runner bundles (runner YAML and MCP JSON). Set to the public URL in prod so exports are launch-ready. | | ` PORT ` | ` 8000 ` | Uvicorn bind port. Cloud Run overrides to its injected ` PORT `. | | ` GCS_BUCKET ` | ` "" ` | GCS bucket for resource uploads. Empty falls back to local filesystem at ` LOCAL_STORAGE_DIR `. | | ` GCS_SA_EMAIL ` | ` "" ` | Service account email for signed-URL generation. Paired with ` GCS_BUCKET `. | | ` LOCAL_STORAGE_DIR ` | ` data/resources ` | Local-disk path for resource uploads when GCS isn't configured. Persist this directory or volume in self-hosted deployments. | | ` GITHUB_TOKEN `, ` GITLAB_TOKEN `, ` GITEA_TOKEN ` | ` "" ` | Last-resort provider tokens when a workspace has no matching stored git connection. Each credential is host-checked; there is no cross-provider fallback. | | ` GITHUB_API_URL ` | ` https://api.github.com ` | GitHub REST base URL, including GitHub Enterprise deployments. | | ` ALLOW_GLOBAL_TOKEN_FALLBACK ` | ` true ` | Allows Git Connections to fall back to the platform token after workspace credentials. Disable it for a strict multi-tenant posture. | | ` GIT_USER_NAME `, ` GIT_USER_EMAIL ` | ` Backplane Merge Bot `, ` merge-bot@valaris.studio ` | Commit identity used by the backend merge worker. | | ` MERGE_QUEUE_STALE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS ` | ` 300 ` | Age after which board health reports a non-terminal merge-queue entry as stale. | | ` INTEGRATIONS_TOKEN_KEY ` | ` "" ` | Base64-encoded 32-byte Fernet key for encrypting the tokens stored by Git Connections. Empty makes token encryption and decryption fail loudly instead of storing plaintext. | | ` GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID `, ` GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET ` | ` "" ` | GitHub OAuth App credentials for workspace git integrations. Empty disables the OAuth start endpoint. | | ` WS_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL ` | ` 30 ` | Seconds between server-sent WebSocket heartbeats. Tune only if you know why. | | ` WS_PONG_TIMEOUT ` | ` 10 ` | Seconds to wait for a client pong before dropping the connection. | ## MCP server Read from ` mcp-server/src/valaris_mcp/config.py `. Set these in the MCP server environment. Claude hosts use the ` mcpServers.valaris.env ` block; exported runner configs and the runner's isolated Codex config pass the same names. | Variable | Default | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | ` VALARIS_API_URL ` | ` http://localhost:8000 ` | Base URL of the Backplane backend. Production is the public backend Cloud Run URL. | | ` VALARIS_API_KEY ` | ` "" ` | Bearer API key (` vlr_... `), either personal or linked to a registered agent. When set, all other auth paths are skipped and ` Authorization: Bearer ` is sent. The simplest production config. | | ` VALARIS_AGENT_EMAIL ` | ` agent@valaris.dev ` | Identity sent in dev-mode auth headers. Ignored when an API key or IAP audience is configured. | | ` VALARIS_IAP_AUDIENCE ` | ` "" ` | Target audience for Google ADC OIDC token minting. Set when the MCP server is talking to an IAP-gated backend without an API key. | | ` VALARIS_MCP_ALLOWLIST ` | unset | Comma-separated tool ids enforced by the MCP server. The allowlist filters both what the model is shown (tools/list) and what it may call. Unset, empty, or ` * ` means unrestricted; ` __none__ ` denies every tool. Invalid names fail server startup rather than silently disabling the gate. | | ` VALARIS_MCP_TOOLSETS ` | ` default ` | Comma-separated toolset ids (group or category ids from the tool catalog) the server lists and serves. Unset or empty means ` default `, the interactive hand; ` all ` loads every tool, which is what runner launches pin. Composes with the allowlist as an intersection; unknown ids fail server startup. | | ` MCP_TRANSPORT ` | ` stdio ` | Switch to ` streamable-http ` to serve over HTTP instead of stdio. | | ` MCP_HOST ` | ` 0.0.0.0 ` | HTTP transport bind address. Ignored for stdio. | | ` MCP_PORT ` | ` 8001 ` | HTTP transport port. Ignored for stdio. | ## The Go runner The runner's primary config is its YAML file. A handful of env vars override YAML values at startup — useful for container deployments where the YAML is a template and the secrets arrive at runtime. | Variable | YAML field it overrides | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | ` VALARIS_API_URL ` | ` valaris.api_url ` | Backend URL the runner authenticates against. Same value the MCP server uses. | | ` VALARIS_API_KEY ` | ` valaris.api_key ` | Bearer key minted for the registered runner. Prefer the env var over committing keys to YAML. | | ` VALARIS_WORKSPACE ` | ` valaris.workspace_slug ` | Workspace scope for the runner. Required through YAML, a named profile, or this override. | | ` VALARIS_WS_ENABLED ` | ` websocket.enabled ` | ` false ` or ` 0 ` force-disables the runner's WebSocket client. Other values do not force-enable it. | | ` VALARIS_NO_SUPERVISOR ` | (debug flag) | ` 1 ` disables panic recovery, matching ` -no-supervisor `. Debug only: a panic terminates the process. | | ` VALARIS_AGENT_EMAIL ` | (MCP child identity) | Inherited by the spawned MCP server for development-header identity. It is not a runner YAML override and is ignored when the MCP server uses an API key or IAP. | | ` ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ` | (not an inherited runner override) | The runner deliberately does not read this env var into config and strips an inherited value before spawning ` claude `. To bill API credits, set ` llm.anthropic_api_key ` in YAML; leave it empty for Claude Max / OAuth. | | ` CODEX_API_KEY ` | (not an inherited runner override) | The Codex driver also strips an inherited key before spawning ` codex `. The current runner config has no general YAML field that wires this provider option, so normal runner execution must use ` codex login ` credentials. | > [!IMPORTANT] > API keys don't belong in committed files > > > > Every env var named ` *_API_KEY ` is a secret. The runner's YAML supports ` ${VALARIS_API_KEY} ` interpolation precisely so the committed config file can stay checked-in while the key flows in at process start. Don't paste a real key into a committed YAML or MCP config just because "it's internal."

en.title: What Works Well
en.markdown: Honest Remarks # What Works Well Backplane's strongest parts are the boundaries that the repository can verify. The backend, frontend, MCP server, and Go Runner live together, and focused contract tests pin the payloads and names they share. That does not make every boundary automatic, but it turns important drift into a test failure instead of an operator surprise. ## The platform owns execution shape The Runner fetches ` pipeline_config ` from the backend and executes the stages that the platform resolved. A registration can carry multiple ` team_roles `, and assignment responses can select a provider and model for the current stage. Pipeline behavior therefore changes through platform configuration rather than a hardcoded role list in the Runner binary. ## Dependencies are an end-to-end feature The ` card_dependencies ` relation is backed by database constraints, cycle validation, scheduler filtering, board and card APIs, frontend management surfaces, and MCP tools. A planner can build a dependency graph and a Runner can avoid work whose prerequisites are not complete without encoding the graph in prose. ## Provider seams execute real implementations The coding-agent seam has working ` claude-cli ` and ` codex-cli ` implementations. The forge seam exposes ` forge.Provider ` and ships GitHub and Gitea/Forgejo drivers. The registries reject unknown provider names instead of silently falling back to a different implementation. ## Event delivery has a scale-aware backend The event API keeps one subscriber contract while ` EVENT_BUS_BACKEND ` selects an in-process memory bus or a ` postgres ` implementation based on PostgreSQL ` LISTEN/NOTIFY `. The health endpoint reports the selected backend and listener state, so cross-instance delivery is observable when it is enabled. > [!PROTIP] > The useful discipline is enforced, not aspirational > > > > Contract tests cover high-risk seams such as MCP signatures, lifecycle kinds, dependency events, localized technical tokens, and Runner wire shapes. The repository still contains ordinary maintenance debt; the strength is that critical invariants have executable checks.

en.title: Known Rough Edges
en.markdown: Honest Remarks # Known Rough Edges These limitations are visible in the current code. They are not a historical audit score, a staffing claim, or a promise that a fix is scheduled.
